news.title: 'This Week' Transcript 11-22-26: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton
news.text:
A rush transcript of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" airing on Sunday, November 22, 2026 on ABC News is below. This copy may not be in its final form, may be updated and may contain minor transcription errors. For previous show transcripts, visit the "This Week" transcript archive.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

JONATHAN KARL, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR: After a week of anxiety over tech outages, we’re now learning of new cyberattacks at the FBI and another federal government agency. “THIS WEEK” starts right now.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: Tech frenzy.

SEN. JOSH HAWLEY (R-MO): If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.

KARL: High-profile outages leave the nation rattled and markets plunging, as the administration tries to calm nerves.

J.D. VANCE, VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Should we be preparing to build a bunker and to stock up on food and water? And my answer to that is, no.

KARL: And lawmakers demand answers.

REP. DANIEL GOLDMAN (D-NY): Is it your testimony today that the American people should believe that the series and sequence of events over the last week is purely coincidental?

JAY CLAYTON, DIRECTOR OF NATIONAL SECURITY: We have no indication that these events are related.

KARL: This morning, we are joined by America’s highest ranking intelligence official, Jay Clayton.

China, Russia and Trump.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: There was great, great electricity. Unbelievable.

KARL: As President Trump touts his meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, backlash at home.

SEN. CHUCK SCHUMER (D-NY): It’s a betrayal of the United States.

KARL: What did the president accomplish? We’re joined by former White House chief of staff, ambassador to Japan, and former mayor of Chicago, Rahm Emanuel.

And Elon’s 180.

ELON MUSK, FOUNDER, TESLA: I’m not MAGA. Well, at least I’m not like -- I'm not sure what MAGA means.

KARL: Our roundtable on Elon Musk’s sudden reversal, as Democrats prepare to take over Congress.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

ANNOUNCER: From ABC News it’s “THIS WEEK.” Here now, Jonathan Karl.

KARL: Good morning. Welcome to “THIS WEEK.”

As we come on the air this morning, we are learning more about apparent cyberattacks on two major government agencies, the FBI and the Department of Agriculture. Unlike the major tech outages that we’ve seen over the past ten days, sources tell ABC News that these are the work of bad actors breaking into government systems, something that will no doubt add to the anxiety that many of us are feeling about the systems we rely on in our everyday lives. The systems that power our economy.

Government officials, from the president to the secretary of state, to the director of national intelligence have told us that all those tech outages were caused by technical glitches, not cyberattacks. That may be true. It’s also true that many Americans just don’t buy it.

Regardless, the vulnerabilities have heightened concerns that bad actors can use the power of artificial intelligence to do significantly more damage. And this week, Anthropic, a company whose CEO has warned that his technology has the potential to destroy all of humanity, went public.

The stock market itself had a brutal week. The Dow and the Nasdaq, the worst week since the Covid pandemic forced the shutdown of much of the country in March of 2020. Some of the anxiety is playing out on the shelves of stores like Costco and Walmart, which have seen a surge in sales of generators, water and other basic supplies you would need in an emergency. While much of this was happening here at home, President Trump traveled to Asia, where he enjoyed a lavish welcome in China and met with the world’s two most powerful dictators. His message to fellow Americans, relax, things will be OK.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

KARL (voice over): An imperial welcome for President Trump in China. President Xi on the red carpet greeting Air Force One. Young performers waving pom poms and flags. The People’s Liberation Army Band. Chinese soldiers marching in formation. And from Xi himself, a hug. Trump called the greeting itself a big win for America.

It was also the third time this year that President Trump has met with China’s president. America’s most powerful adversary, and a man Trump calls his friend.

And Trump also met with the other dictator he calls a friend, relishing his elaborate three-way meeting with Putin and Xi. The first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States. A memorable photo-op for sure, the Chinese president presiding, but no major accomplishments beyond providing a distraction from the growing anxiety back home.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Tell them to relax. Everything’s good.

KARL (voice over): A nation on edge over artificial intelligence. A seemingly endless onslaught of major tech outages. And a tanking stock market.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Now to the major sell-off in A.I. stocks.

KARL (voice over): This week, the biggest IPO in history. Anthropic valued momentarily at $2 trillion. The excitement quickly gave way to anxiety. The worst week for the Dow and the Nasdaq since the Covid pandemic shut the country down more than six years ago, hammering the 401(k)s of millions of Americans.

Investor fear on Wall Street mirrored growing apprehension on main street. Tech outages seemingly everywhere, messing with air travel, banking, email and even the nation’s most secretive spy agency. The Trump administration tried to quell those concerns, saying none of it appeared to be the work of a nefarious hacker.

MARCO RUBIO, SECRETARY OF STATE: We have absolutely no reason to believe, we have no evidence, no indications of any kind that these instances -- that these incidents are related to each other.

JAY CLAYTON, DIRECTOR OF NATIONAL SECURITY: They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.

KARL (voice over): But that was before the cyberattacks on the FBI and the Department of Agriculture late last week. And one tech leader is warning that cyberattackers will soon overwhelm those trying to defend against them.

PALMER LUCKEY, ANDURIL INDUSTRIES FOUNDER: And as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers, who are very fast moving and using technology, and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed. And I think it’s -- people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

KARL: And I'm joined now by America's top-ranked intelligence official, director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton.

Director Clayton, thank you for being with us here this morning.

Let me start right with the -- these reports of a recent hack to the FBI’s criminal database. What can you tell us about that?

JAY CLAYTON, DIRECTOR OF NATIONAL SECURITY: Jon, let me -- let me put it in context. And there’s been a lot of discussion this week about our cybersecurity, our digital infrastructure.

Cyber probing, cyber incidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time. And what we’re hearing about the FBI, and what I've -- what I've talked to them about is they have an incident. They’re dealing with it in the ordinary course.

Let me -- let me give you some data here, Jon. In 2020, there were roughly 750,000 cyber incidents reported to the FBI. That’s now up to over a million cyber incidents. And what we’re seeing, though, here, and I want the American people to know this, is we have a step change in technology that we’re facing with superintelligence and computing power that is expanding exponentially and we have a dated digital infrastructure. The need to improve our digital infrastructure is clear. And that is -- that is the dynamic that we have today.

KARL: So, you don’t see this as a particularly alarming attack? This isn’t an attack reported by the FBI. This is an attack on the FBI. But this doesn’t seem like -- do we have any idea who’s behind it?

CLAYTON: Jon, I'm not in a position to get into the specifics right now on that, what I would say is incident. We have highly professional people at the FBI who handle both private sector and public sector incidents like this. And I'm sure we’ll get the answers in due course, just as we’ve gotten the answers to the incidents that happened this past week at the NSA, at Microsoft, at other places.

You know, one of the great things about America, and going into Thanksgiving week I always remind everybody about this, is transparency is key. We gather the facts and then we share them with the American people. And that’s what will happen here.

KARL: And you remain confident that all those other incidents that we’ve seen, beginning with Microsoft, the FAA, J.P. Morgan, all of those other incidents, those were technical glitches. Those were not cyberattacks. But the FBI incident is different. And also, we heard about this Department of Agriculture incident. What can you tell us about that? Do you have any information about who was behind that hack?

CLAYTON: Again, not getting into specifics.

Let me tell you what we know and be very clear with the American people. The incidents that we saw during the course of this week, we know that they were not coordinated and that they were not state sponsored. These were -- these were what I would say is delays, outages and the like resulting from upgrades to systems which are absolutely necessary going forward. And we’re going to see more of that. And companies and the government, we should all be transparent with the American people that we have dated systems in a highly evolving environment where they need to be upgraded in order to have cybersecurity.

Now, to your point on cyberattacks -- there is an increase, as I mentioned, in cyberattacks. But this is something that we have had for a long time. Many of our companies -- let me -- let me make a great point about America. We have the leading cybersecurity firms in America. And these are large firms. The reason they’re large firms is that this has been an issue that we’ve been dealing with and dealing with on the front foot for a while.

If you look at the leading independent cybersecurity firms in America, they have a market cap, $200 billion, $300 billion. That’s the amount of effort and ingenuity and human capital that we’ve been putting into these things. We are going to lead the world in protecting digital infrastructure, Jon.

KARL: Let me turn to China. Senator Tom Cotton, I'm sure you saw, told “The Wall Street Journal” this week that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings about A.I. chips being smuggled into China.

He said, “If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about the Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously.”

Cotton says that the administration, “although they took some steps,” you took some steps, “this week on this issue,” he says, “it’s just a big late, regrettably, and I think we need to catalogue the damage that has already been done.”

So, is Tom Cotton right, there’s been damage that’s been done because of what’s not gone through at Commerce, and how much damage?

CLAYTON: Let’s take this back and frame it for the American people. We have export restrictions on exquisite technology. They are restrictions. They are not bans.

What do we want as the American people? We want to absolutely maintain our leadership in exquisite technology. That means not allowing our adversaries to gain access to that.

However, we also want to lead in technology infrastructure around the world. So that means that less exquisite technology should be available around the globe for this digital infrastructure buildout. The Department of Commerce, the Department of Treasury, they are -- they are in the business of metering that. And I will leave the specifics of that to them.

KARL: I mean, he’s saying quite directly that Howard Lutnick ignored his warnings and did damage to the country’s national security as a result. Is Tom Cotton wrong about that?

CLAYTON: Jon, what I'm going to -- what I'm going to say is, in that context of, we want to lead the globe in the buildout of this infrastructure, but we also want to keep the most exquisite capabilities for America. There is -- there is a debate to be had. And I -- and I support that discussion.

KARL: OK, I don’t hear a direct answer to that, but let me -- let me move to the other related major issue if you can clear something up for me on the Nvidia question, the Nvidia question. Did Alice Huang, the woman who reportedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, did she pass on information or otherwise assist the Chinese communist government?

CLAYTON: Jon, as Attorney General Blanche has made clear, there is an investigation ongoing into her firm and into her. And I'm going to await the outcome of that investigation.

KARL: Can you say with confidence that Nvidia chips were not used to support the Chinese military?

CLAYTON: Oh, Jon, let’s be clear. Nvidia chips are -- they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants. That’s why we’re focusing on this.

People will do a lot. They will break the law. There are indictments already involving other companies where people have broken the law to get access to Nvidia chips.

That is -- that is why it is so important for us to lead and for us to understand how we meter access around the world.

KARL: Do you know where Alice Huang is right now?

CLAYTON: Jon, I can’t tell you that. I do not.

KARL: You do not. There are reports that she is in China.

CLAYTON: Oh.

KARL: Let me ask you another question about the president’s recent trip this week to China. He called Vladimir Putin a “friend,” which he’s done before, and then he posted this on Truth Social, a picture of -- with Vladimir Putin saying, “my friend.” And when he was asked about this, this week, he was asked, “he’s your friend. Is he America's friend?” The president said, “I can’t speak to America.”

But let me ask you. You’re the director of National Intelligence. Is Vladimir Putin America's friend?

CLAYTON: That conversation, that picture, historic, historic picture, was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers getting together and saying, we cannot have a -- we cannot have a nuclear incident.

That’s -- it’s unbelievable that the three of them got together and had that discussion in what I -- what I would say is, you know, a time in the world where there’s conflict and the like and it should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying, we’re not going to go in that direction.

KARL: But my -- but my --

CLAYTON: I think -- I think that any time you have that it’s -- but let me say, in that --

CLAYTON: In that circle -- in that circle of that conversation, using the term “friend” is entirely appropriate.

KARL: So, but my question is, is Vladimir Putin America's friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question.

CLAYTON: Look, I -- Jon --

KARL: Is he America's friend?

CLAYTON: Jon, is Vladimir Putin America's friend? He is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all.

KARL: OK. And let me ask you, we -- this week we -- you know, as you know, the -- CISA, the cybersecurity agency, has been without a confirmed leader for almost two years now, but we finally did have a nominee who had a confirmation hearing this week. This is Michael LoSapio. I want to play something from that hearing for you.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

SEN. RICHARD BLUMENTHAL (D-CT): Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021?

MICHAEL LOSAPIO, CISA DIRECTOR NOMINEE: I don’t know.

BLUMENTHAL: You don’t know?

LOSAPIO: I don’t know how you define --

BLUMENTHAL: Really?

LOSAPIO: So, I -- no, I don’t believe it was an attack, no.

BLUMENTHAL: Let me ask you again. I'll give you another chance. January 6, 2021, was the Capitol attacked?

LOSAPIO: No.

BLUMENTHAL: It was not attacked?

LOSAPIO: No, sir.

news.title: Report: AOC and Kamala Harris Are the 'X-Factor' in the 2028 Presidential Primary Contest
news.text:
With the midterms only a few weeks in the rearview mirror attention has already turned to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, where one news outlet reported it was ready “to explode into sprawling, wide-open field.”

That was the conclusion of an NBC News analysis on Saturday of the contest two years away, with the network pointing out that anyone with a notion of running for president first must navigate the presence of high-profile Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and former VP and failed 2024 candidate Kamala Harris.

As NBC described the challenge:

Both are known universally within their party, have demonstrated the ability to raise ungodly sums of money and rank at or near the top in early polls — standards that most presidential hopefuls will never achieve.
And both take up commanding lanes of the electorate. Harris, the former vice president, won 75 million votes as the party’s nominee in 2024 and 92% of Black women voters. Ocasio-Cortez, a congresswoman from New York, is widely perceived to be the heir to the progressive populist movement built by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.

Yet, neither women have expressed their intentions for 2028, which looms as an “X factor” for other potential candidates as they begin to devise their campaign strategies.

“It fundamentally changes the dynamics of the primary. They are the ones sitting on the biggest blocs,” veteran Democratic pollster Celinda Lake told NBC. “They have total name recognition. Despite all the controversies — they are actually well-liked by key constituencies of a Democratic primary.”

Lake has polled in the past for Ocasio-Cortez. She said both women candidates would generate a “fundamental reshuffling of the coalitions, of the targeting strategies, of the themes, of what people will be looking for, who is considered viable and not.”

RELATED: The Return of Rambling Kamala

The network apparently surveyed more than 20 Democratic “strategists, pollsters and elected officials” who pointed out any candidate faced a “minefield” if Cortez or Harris launch campaigns. They also said that if neither funs, the competition will be to win their endorsements.

Lake pointed out that Harris’ popularity with Black women makes her an immediate threat, particularly in the influential South Carolina primary early in the nomination calendar. Harris has been coy about her intentions, as she was about running for California governor, which she ultimately declined to do.

Just elected to a fifth term in the House, Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a bid for the presidency but is also exploring a run in 2028 for the New York Senate seat currently occupied by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.

If both women stay out of the race, NBC reported, it could leave the field without a female candidate, though Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) has expressed an interest in running.

According to exit polling, the midterm wins were generated by woman, with 60 percent of female voters supporting the Democratic choices on the ballot.

RELATED: JD Vance Roasts AOC for Her Biden Brain-Freeze for “20 Seconds” on World Stage

One unnamed Democratic strategist who advised statewide candidates in the midterms put the problem in the simplest of terms.

Said the consultant, “Everyone’s waiting on Kamala and AOC. They’ll be building [their campaigns] around the two of them.”

news.title: Crypto CEOs Who Spent the Last Few Years Bootlicking Trump Are Now Stumbling Over Themselves to Proclaim Their Allegiance to the Democratic Party
news.text:
The grifters and hucksters emboldened by Donald Trump are now tripping over themselves to curry favor with the incoming Democratic majority in Congress. Chief among them are the titans of the crypto industry, whose businesses have achieved something akin to institutional legitimacy under the last few years of Republican rule.

But things are looking tense for the blockchain crowd now, after industry spending groups burned some $200 million backing Republican candidates in the US midterms in efforts that decidedly failed to pay off.

In particular, crypto lobbyists went all-out to defeat now-incoming Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, spending over $55 million on his race alone. It’s now Brown’s second stare-down with the blockchain barons, and according to reporting by Politico, many Democrats aren’t in a forgiving mood.

As pro-crypto Democratic senator Ruben Gallego put it: “they’re f**ked.”

The tone from crypto trade groups is now meeker than arguably ever before. CEO of the crypto firm Digital Chamber Cody Carbone told Politico that the industry needs to pivot from antagonizing Democrats to embracing “an education-first mindset.”

Carbone added that the midterm elections were a “wake-up call” for crypto lobbyists and the companies they champion, and that the industry needs to “lean into both sides equally.”

And as Sheila Warren, the former CEO of an industry firm called the Crypto Council for Innovation told Politico, the lobby’s financial war on Democrats like Ohio’s SHerrod Brown was “boneheaded.”

“So it looks like just a show of force,” Warren explained, “and that’s never a good look, especially when you lose.”

All that said, the degree to which Democratic leadership will seek to antagonize the crypto lobby in 2027 is still up in the air. The last days of the Biden administration were marked by Democratic moves to cozy up to the industry, with a coalition forming to urge then-Vice President Kamala Harris to adopt a more pro-crypto stance. 

For her part, Harris seemed to have acquiesced. During her ill-fated presidential run in 2024, she announced a bizarre policy move to push crypto on Black men — an initiative largely viewed as the Democratic establishment’s capitulation in the face of massive industry spending on Harris’s campaign.

news.title: Buoyed by midterms, Democrats start looking to 2028
news.text: Since Democrats' landslide victories in this month's midterm elections, the party has been consumed by a near-term task — how to quickly deliver promised relief to Americans when the new Congress convenes in January. Alongside that effort is the longer-term conversation about how to capture the White House in 2028 and who will vie to carry the party's mantle. Top Democrats have yet to announce candidacies, and the party is still basking in its historic victories. Nevertheless, the two weeks following the midterms have seen a flurry of activity, including a conference in Denver where more than a dozen influential Democrats laid out ideas for the party's future. "Democrats across the country feel really good. That has prompted a lot of conversations about where to go from here and what does 2028 look like," said Joe Caiazzo, a Democratic strategist who worked on the presidential campaigns of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). On Thursday, allies of former Vice President Kamala Harris launched a draft committee urging her to run. Such committees have also sprung up postelection for Silicon Valley Rep. Ro Khanna, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. "There's mass amounts of energy," Matthew Taylor, who is heading the Harris-aligned draft committee, said of the general party mood. "Democrats have big, bold plans on what we want to accomplish, and we can't accomplish that without 2028 — and the process does start now." Sen. Alex Padilla of California, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Buttigieg have announced forthcoming books. And various figures have planned travel stops, including New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, who was in South Carolina on Friday, and Harris, who was reported to have a Friday meeting in Paris with French President Emmanuel Macron. California Gov. Gavin Newsom likewise has continued efforts to cast himself as an alternative to President Trump on the world and domestic stages, making a surprise trip to Ukraine after attending the United Nations conference on climate change in Turkey. Newsom then headed to Capitol Hill, where on Wednesday he unveiled an AI framework, addressed national anxiety following tech outages and made jabs at the "lack of leadership" in Washington under Trump. The 2028 presidential election will be a race to chart America's course after a decade that has been dominated by Trump, and it will be the first presidential race in which both parties have wide-open primaries since 2016. For Democrats, the chance to wrest back control of the White House after their bruising 2024 loss carries stakes many view as existential. "They are absolutely determined to win, because most Democrats feel that Trump has done worse harm to this country than any president in anybody's memory," said Elaine Kamarck, director of the Brookings Institution's Center for Effective Public Management and the author of a book on primary politics. "They're absolutely ready to win, and I think you saw that in the way people ran their 2026 races." Throughout the midterm campaign season, likely contenders traveled the country to meet voters and stump for Democratic candidates, helping boost their own visibility in key swing states while working as party surrogates. Now, potential contenders have a window of time before declaring their candidacies to hire staff, talk to party leaders in various states — chatter has already emerged about which hopefuls made calls to new Democratic stars after the midterms — and court fundraisers and donors. "It does feel like the shadow primary is underway," said Jim Demers, a veteran Democratic strategist in New Hampshire, traditionally a testing ground for presidential hopefuls. "I would expect that after the first of the year, we will see the pace pick up, sort of like shifting into the next gear." The Democratic field is expected to be large; jokes about whether all the contenders will fit on the debate stage abound. While the supporters behind draft committees are lining up for their picks, many party activists and donors are interested in a robust primary. "Talking to a lot of our activists here, people are not ready to make any early commitments," Demers said. "They are very much wanting to see the field, hear them and then make their decision." In a poll released this month pitting various Democrats against Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who are widely seen as possible Republican front-runners, the Democratic candidate was favored over Vance or Rubio by voters surveyed in seven swing states. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff led the pack, up 9 points over the Republicans, on average. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear followed, all favored by 7 points, according to the survey, conducted by Impact Research with Equis Research and HIT Strategies. Of California's possible contenders, surveyed voters favored Khanna over Vance or Rubio by 3 percentage points on average, Newsom by 2 points and Harris by 1. Ocasio-Cortez was the only Democrat named in the survey who tied on average with Vance or Rubio rather than outperforming them. Another poll from Reuters/Ipsos showed Ossoff, Buttigieg, Vance and Rubio as the top 2028 contenders. Of Republican voters polled, 45% said Rubio would be an excellent candidate and 43% said Vance would; of Democratic voters polled, 29% each said the same of Buttigieg and Ossoff. The Republican conversation has largely centered on Vance and Rubio, though figures outside the Trump administration such as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz are also viewed as positioned for possible runs. How the party advances without Trump at the top of the ticket, and whether voters choose to follow the MAGA path or deviate, will be key questions in the GOP primary. In the days since the midterms, leaders across the Democratic political spectrum have agreed — and warned — that the party must deliver results in the next Congress in order to retain the swing voters who gave them the blue wave. The party will need to succeed at "getting something done" in Washington in order to win loyalty from voters who backed blue candidates in this month's elections out of dissatisfaction with the GOP rather than out of affinity for Democrats, said Luke Nichter, chair of presidential studies at Chapman University. "The strategy there is to convert voters who were voting against something," Nichter said, "who maybe in 2028 can vote for something."
news.summary: The 2028 presidential election will be a race to chart America's course after a decade that has been dominated by President Trump.
news.author: Justine McDaniel

news.title: Barabak: A blue Texas is a monumental shift. That's already reshaping the 2028 presidential race
news.text: In 2020, when Joe Biden came within 5 percentage points of winning Texas, it was cause for Democratic celebration. Biden, en route to the White House, turned in the strongest performance by a Democratic presidential candidate in a quarter-century, More promising, it seemed as though he'd built on Hillary Clinton's showing in 2016, when she lost the state by 9 points. Visions of a blue Texas danced before eager Democratic eyes. Then came 2024. Donald Trump clobbered Kamala Harris by double digits. Texas — fast-growing, demographically changing — had long stymied Democrats, who believed the booming Latino population, in particular, guaranteed success. The state was a chimera, a blue mirage, a plum that always lay beyond the party's plucking. Until Nov. 3. In one of the most stunning outcomes in a midterm election filled with jaw-dropping surprises, Democrats captured each and every one of the top statewide offices in Texas, claimed a U.S. Senate seat, flipped the House of Representatives and defeated all four Republicans seeking reelection to the state Supreme Court. This after failing to win a single statewide office in more than 30 years. But the GOP drubbing is not just something for Democrats to crow about. The red-to-blue transformation represents a monumental shift that carries nationwide implications, not least in reshaping the 2028 presidential race. "There's a lot of levels," said Mike Madrid, a Republican strategist and expert on the Latino vote. "There's the narrative. There's morale. There's demographics. There's the road map to 270," the number of electoral votes it takes to win the White House. Only a fool would venture to say how Texas — which hasn't gone Democratic in a presidential election since 1976 — will vote two years from now. (Don't look at me like that.) Especially based on the outcome of a single, extraordinary election. Much will depend on the presidential nominees, how much they raise and where, when the screws tighten, the candidates and their allies choose to allocate their time and money. But the plain fact is Republicans can no longer assume Texas is all locked up, as they have for well over a generation. To do so would be suicidal, said Dave Carney, a campaign strategist for the state's last two governors, Rick Perry and Greg Abbott. The GOP, Carney said, is "going to have to have a command focus" to win back the state in 2028. That alone is a huge development and, potentially, the most significant change to the presidential map since 1992, when another reliably Republican state turned blue — for the next 30 years it turned out, and counting. When Bill Clinton won California in 1992, he became the first Democrat to do so since Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964. It wasn't a particularly impressive victory. Clinton carried the state with just 46% of the vote in a three-way contest with President George H.W. Bush and independent Ross Perot. Many, including Clinton and those around him, feared the showing might be a one-off, with California reverting to Republican form at the first opportunity. So Clinton devoted the next four years to solidifying his support, lavishing money and endless attention on California, which helped turn the state into the blue bastion we know today. In 1996, Clinton crushed Republican Bob Dole by 13 percentage points. No Republican has come close to winning the state since; few presidential candidates have even tried to compete. That effective GOP surrender was hugely consequential. It freed Democrats to spend hundreds of millions of dollars elsewhere, including the battlegrounds of the Midwest and states such as Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, North Carolina and Virginia. which once seemed beyond reach. Now the opposite is true. Money and resources that Republicans might have devoted to other states may need to be invested in Texas, an enormously expensive state which, for decades, has been foundational to the GOP's presidential success. The state's 40 electoral votes are second only to California, which has 54. It's hard to see how Republicans make up that deficit if they fail to carry Texas. There's been a self-defeating, self-perpetuating cycle that vexed Democrats for years. Winning Texas seemed like an extreme long shot at the presidential level, so the party and its candidates refused to invest the considerable sum needed to make the state competitive. Because they declined to make that investment, the state never grew truly competitive. With Democrats in control in Austin and the state's incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, and U.S. senator, James Talarico, positioned to bulk up the party's fundraising and organizational muscle, those days are over. It's not, however, as if Texas suddenly leans Democratic. Hinojosa and Talarico are both relative moderates, especially compared with most blue-state Democrats, which explains at least some of their success. "Do I think [California Gov.] Gavin Newsom has a chance of carrying Texas? No," said Karl Rove, who worked to turn the state into a Republican fortress before helping put Gov. George W. Bush to the White House. "Do I think [Illinois Gov.] JB Pritzker has a chance? No. Do I think someone who's a centrist could? It depends who the Republican is. "The further left the candidate, the less likely it is they're going to be competitive in this state," Rove said. "The larger their wallet, the more likely it is they can afford to come in and play." John Anzalone, a Democratic pollster who has worked in several presidential campaigns, including Biden's 2020 run, agreed it's far too soon to size up the 2028 landscape. What is clear, Anzalone said, is that after statewide wins in places such as Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi "the electoral battleground map has expanded" and Democrats "will be spending in states [where] we haven't spent in a long time." Also clear: Texas is no longer a certain Democratic heartbreaker, beckoning but invariably falling outside their reach.
news.summary: It's been 50 years since a Democrat won the state, but after a midterm blowout Texas is now competitive. The shift is the most significant change to the presidential map since California went blue.
news.author: Mark Z. Barabak

news.title: Why the U.S. midterms might have ended JD Vance's presidential hopes
news.text:
JD Vance's presidential ambitions for 2028 could be among the most significant political casualties of the Democratic blue wave in this month's U.S. midterm elections.

His chances of becoming the Republican candidate in two years may have suffered a more recent blow, as reports suggest U.S. President Donald Trump has begun to sour on his vice-president.

"Despite years of work to keep his feet glued to Trump’s MAGA coattails, [Vance] is probably losing any semblance of hope that he’ll get to be a GOP frontrunner in 2028," New York Intelligencer staff editor Chas Danner wrote in an article under the headline "JD Vance’s presidential dream is being snuffed out."

"At the beginning of the year, Vance was widely seen as the GOP’s presumptive 2028 nominee. He may end the year as the presumptive also-ran, if that."

Over at the conservative magazine National Review, senior writer Noah Rothman also weighed in on what he views as Vance's diminishing political fortunes, saying, "Those who invested in JD Vance’s political stock ... may be looking to offload their holdings."

AnalysisJD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

Vance hasn’t publicly said if he will run for president in 2028, but before the midterms, he was considered a front-runner, with perhaps the highest name recognition of any potential candidate. 

However, since the midterms, Vance's aspirations "have suffered, because he's Donald Trump's vice-president," said Michael Traugott, a research professor emeritus at the University of Michigan's Center for Political Studies, in an interview with CBC News.

Exit polls suggested Republicans lost the election over issues relating to inflation and the cost of living, government corruption and the war in Iran.

"The problem is that the vice-president can't separate himself very easily from the administration's policies," Traugott said.

Donors express concerns about Vance

According to the Wall Street Journal, after the Democrats' success in taking the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms, some Republican donors began making calls to senior party members and expressing concerns that they couldn't back Vance, because he's too tied to an unpopular administration.

This illustrates the challenge Vance faces: Do Republican primary voters want a candidate who has broader support among the general public but isn't directly connected to the president, or will they only support someone who has Trump's endorsement?

"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist, told Reuters.

Trump hasn’t endorsed Vance or anyone else. Reports have also emerged recently that Vance himself is not so sure about a run, particularly in the wake of the Republicans' disastrous showing in the midterms.

In Republican primaries, Trump still commands a lot of votes and a lot of respect, Martin Cohen, a political science professor with James Madison University, told CBC News.

"I would definitely think that the front-runner would be the candidate with Trump's endorsement, if he does give one," he said.

Vance blamed Iran war for midterm losses

That means Vance will have to get his boss's approval, as well as the support of the MAGA base, while "trying to distance himself a little bit, at least," Cohen said.

Vance's attempt to distance himself from the administration may have already begun, with possible consequences. Following the midterms, Vance, in a lengthy post on X, levelled much of the blame for Republican losses on the war in Iran.

"If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest."

Vance, who according to reports has for a while privately expressed reservations about the war, has simultaneously argued that there's "no daylight" between him and the president on Iran. 

In response to the X post, Trump agreed Iran may have been a factor in the midterm losses. But he also insisted that invading Iran was the right policy decision.

Trump told reporters that Vance's post should have added, "'If you had it to do again, would you do it again?' The answer is yes."

Soon after the X post, the vice-president, who had been leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, was taken off the file. 

Posting on Truth Social, Trump said his administration no longer needed a deal with Iran and that he wanted Vance to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.

Why the war in Iran might cost Trump and the Republicans at the ballot boxWhat the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

Abe Greenwald, the executive editor of Commentary magazine, called Trump's sidelining of Vance a "remarkably skillful work of public humiliation."

Karen Beckwith, a political science professor with Ohio-based Case Western Reserve University, said in an email to CBC News that Trump's removal of Vance from any responsibility for negotiating or interacting with Iranian counterparts "undermines Vance as a potential presidential nominee in 2028."

Meanwhile, Fox News host Brian Kilmeade lashed out at Vance after his interview with Kilmeade's colleague Laura Ingraham, in which Vance said there were some who want the Iran war to go on indefinitely.

Kilmeade rejected that assertion, calling it "another straw man" argument from Vance, while adding that "he never should have been vice-president."

Trump reportedly frustrated with Vance

Beckwith said this could leave Vance without any substantive achievements on which to campaign for the 2028 nomination — unlike potential opponents like Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Republican governors and senators.

Asked about his social media post about Iran at a news conference on Friday, Vance, flanked by both Trump and Rubio, said the president makes the decision, that the president has said he would attack Iran again and that it's his job to support the president.

Vance's comments followed a New York Times report earlier this week that Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how Vance has framed his assessment of what went wrong in Iran, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran.

According to the Times, Trump has instead been praising Rubio, a strong supporter of the U.S. war against Iran, as a potential presidential candidate.

While past polls have shown Vance as the leading Republican candidate for 2028, a recent poll from Emerson College had Rubio as the top choice.

Vance hasn’t publicly said if he will run for president in 2028, but before the midterms, he was considered a front-runner, with perhaps the highest name recognition of any potential candidate.

news.title: PBS Tosses Softballs at Gov. Shapiro, No Zinger on Internal Democrat Battle on Israel
news.text:
The PBS News Hour loves interviewing Democrats. We found earlier this year that they are more than five times as likely to interview a liberal rather than a conservative. On Friday, PBS anchor Amna Nawaz brought on Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-Penn.) to kick off speculation about whether Shapiro is running for president in 2028.

The first softball in the 11-minute interview was this one: "So I got to ask you, what's the governor of Pennsylvania doing delivering a speech on foreign policy if he's not running for president?"

Then on Iran, it’s that type of question that Democrats get, as in “explain what you would do.”

NAWAZ: On the war in Iran, you also mentioned in your speech that you think these midterm wins for Democrats give you an opportunity to develop a new foreign policy. You say you want Democrats to use their new majorities to try to end this Iran war.What does that specifically look like? What kind of legislation can they be passing, especially when they don't have a veto-proof majority?

Then came a question on Israel, but it was very soft. It’s PBS, so there was no attempt to pit Shapiro against Abdul el-Sayed or Mehdi Hasan or Hasan Piker on the allegation that the Jews are running/ruining the world. Nawaz could have cited a quote, like she cited Shapiro's take on Trump a few minutes before: "The chaos, the cruelty, the corruption of this administration has made the U.S. less secure at home and abroad."

In January, Piker rambled on his Twitch stream when The New York Times reported that Shapiro revealed in his new memoir that the Kamala Harris campaign, in vetting Shapiro as a potential running mate in 2024, asked the governor if he had ever been an agent of the Israeli government. Shapiro was offended by the question. So PBS was never going to go there. 

NAWAZ: There's another big issue that continues to really divide members of your party, in particular, and that is the U.S. approach and support for the state of Israel.You saw earlier this year a number of Senate Democrats, including many folks who are sort of eying a 2028 run, voting to block some arms sales to Israel. Would you support efforts like that? And would you have voted with them?

Shapiro struck a politician’s balance:

SHAPIRO: Look, I think, in many ways, this issue is being resolved. You saw before that the president and the current prime minister in Israel have indicated that they are planning to end the military aid that's existed for decades to Israel. I support that. I think it is important to end that military aid.I do think it is important for Israel to be able to have the weapons they need to defend themselves from attacks from terrorist organizations, be it Hamas, the Houthis, the Iranians. And why do I think that? Because it's in America's national security interest.

Nawaz then moved on to Canada, no need to dwell on Israel. But Netanyahu wants a longer timeline for the end of military aid, phasing it out over five or ten years, well beyond 2028. 

Later she asked the blue-wave celebration question:

NAWAZ: We're just coming off these historic Democratic wins in the midterm elections, the blue wave, the blue tsunami, whatever you want to call it. Your reelection win in particular was even bigger than your last by 22 points.But we also saw Democrats win statewide in places like Kansas and Mississippi and South Carolina and the Senate races on that front. How much of your win do you believe was because of you, because of Josh Shapiro, and how much was part of this blue wave?

Shapiro agreed: "Well, it was obviously a great night for Democrats and a complete rejection, not just of Donald Trump, but his enablers." Nawaz then joked "I know you like to talk about getting stuff done, that GSD." Shapiro joked back: "It's PBS, so we'll say stuff, yes." How cozy. 

Shapiro then suggested his first priority in the new term is more than doubling the minimum wage in Pennsylvania, from $7.25 an hour to "at least 15 bucks an hour." He said that would be the first bill crossing his desk.

With 2028 speculation about to hit a fever pitch, reports have indicated that she has been considering her options carefully, with some suggesting that she might be more interested in making a run for Chuck Schumer's Senate seat in New York before going after the presidency.

With the midterm blowout in the rearview, the Republican Party has no choice but to shift its focus to 2028. “Trump has done a lot of great work, the best work that we've ever seen in terms of the big-picture civilizational issues, but unfortunately, the people are not so focused on that. The people are focused on affordability and gas prices,” he adds.

If he becomes the 2028 nominee, Vance, he argues, will have to “walk this tightrope where you're embracing certain parts of MAGA while distancing yourself from the bad parts that the wider population isn't so hot about.”

“That's not going to be easy to do,” Doyle says. “After all, if he attempts to distance himself too much from certain aspects of Trump 47, he risks the problem that sometimes Donald Trump doesn't like that, right? He might get some Truth Social posts about him.”

But that’s not Vance’s only issue, he says.

“A bigger problem, though, is maybe voters will wonder, wait a minute, you were in office — why didn't you do things differently? This is the same problem that Kamala Harris encountered in 2024, right?” Doyle says.

“It's like it was obvious the Biden administration had failed in so many ways. Naturally, Kamala Harris had to try to kind of like distance herself from that, but as we saw, it didn't work. Voters associated her correctly with this disastrous Brandon administration. That's the position Vance finds himself in,” he continues.

Doyle clarifies that he’s not “comparing the disastrous nature of the Brandon admin to the Trump admin” but rather making the point that “it is very difficult to distance yourself from an administration in which you were the second in command.”

The good news is that Vance still has two years to put himself in the best position to run in 2028.

news.title: Justice Alito Warns That Democrats Could Destroy the Supreme Court Forever
news.text:
Democrats have made it abundantly clear that they feel entitled to power, and they're willing to blow up longstanding institutions to get it.

Just look at the filibuster. Under President George W. Bush, Democrats abused it to block judicial nominees and legislation, insisting it was a necessary tool to protect the minority party. When Republicans used the filibuster the same way to stop Barack Obama's agenda, Democrats suddenly decided it was a racist relic of the Jim Crow era. Then, like clockwork, they had no qualms wielding it against President Donald Trump's agenda.

Senate rules aren't the only institution they're willing to change, though.

Ever since conservative justices took a majority on the Supreme Court, Democrats have openly plotted to pack it the moment a Democrat president gives them the chance. They would add as many seats as it takes to install a near-permanent radical-left majority. Their fury has grown every time that majority does its job. The court ended racist affirmative action in college admissions, reined in the power of federal agencies, and, of course, ended the nationwide right to abortion.

Democrats used to be coy about their intentions. In 2020, Joe Biden refused to say whether he would pack the court; then, upon taking office, he set the wheels in motion to do just that. He assembled a commission to give himself political cover for expanding the bench.

It backfired.

Biden's hand-picked commission shot down the idea. It warned that adding seats for partisan purposes would set up an infinite cycle of court expansions, with each new majority simply packing the court with its own. A future Democrat president won't be bothering with a commission; he'll just pack the court.

Do you think Democrats took the hint? They didn't.

The next time Democrats have the votes, they'll pack the court.

If Republicans wanted to, they could nuke the filibuster and pass that law. Unfortunately, Senate Republicans, particularly the leadership, are spineless. So what happens when Democrats take over Congress in January, as they're preparing to do?

The threat to politicize the court is all too real.

Alito knows what's coming.

A party that tears up every rule standing between it and power will never stop. Democrats will change the rules of legislative bodies, remake the court, and even completely overhaul our elections to become a permanent majority.

news.title: Dems Grapple With A Wide-Open Presidential Race — And No Clear Front-Runner
news.text:
Welcome to the most wide-open Democratic presidential primary in two decades.

Party operatives looking at the potential field of candidates (and often trying to get a job with said candidates) do not see a juggernaut waiting to bully the rest of the field. Instead, they see a “Big Five”: Former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. 

But of those five, it’s unclear if three of them — Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff — will end up running at all.

The result is a (very) early race with absolutely no clear frontrunner, a far cry from former President Joe Biden’s pole position in 2020 or former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s clear early dominance in both 2008 and 2016. 

“There’s no clear frontrunner, and even high name ID isn’t necessarily going to translate to success,” said Josh Schwerin, a Democratic strategist with extensive presidential campaign experience, adding: “The eventual nominee is going to have to salvage the terrible reputation of the Democratic Party, and the primary is shaping up to be a very healthy debate about who is the best leader for that challenge.”

Most close observers of the race do not expect candidates to start entering the race in earnest until March. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is widely expected to be the first person to enter the contest, though he has said he won’t make a final decision until after the holidays. At a recent Democratic-run gathering in Denver, most of the rumored potential candidates seemed to kick the tires, sheepishly declaring that they should be the chosen leader.

And of the five leading contenders, it’s unclear whether a majority even want the job. 

Ossoff has publicly ruled out the prospect and committed to serving his full six-year term, citing his desire to spend time with his young family. Ocasio-Cortez has a choice between running for president or running for the U.S. Senate seat held by incoming Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, with many Democrats in New York expecting she’ll prefer the latter. And Harris ― who leads most early primary polls ― has not publicly indicated an announcement timeline, though nearly a dozen of her former aides are now on her payroll, according to independent reporter Zohreen Shah.

Earlier this week, former second gentleman Douglas Emoff said Harris is currently reflecting and will share more in her own time.

“She was really heartened to listen, to hear what people had to say, to support different types of candidates up and down the ticket, not just at the national level, but at the state and local level,” Emhoff said at an event in Los Angeles. “All these offices matter. And that’s what she spent her time doing. And now she’s going to reflect and make a decision, and you’ll all hear it when you hear it.”

The other two leading candidates, Newsom and Buttigieg, are seen as near-certain to run. Buttigieg announced earlier this week he will release a book in January. Newsom has said he won’t run if Harris does — which most Democrats have interpreted as an implicit prediction that Harris will not. Both are seen as flawed leaders, with questions about Buttigieg’s ability to appeal to Black and Latino voters and murmurs that Newsom’s stock peaked a year ago.

A second tier of candidates is moving more aggressively towards a bid. A top aide to Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) recently left Giffords — the gun control group named after his wife — to advise him directly again, while Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro gave a foreign policy-focused speech in Philadelphia on Friday. 

But right now the most active efforts are coming from draft groups not directly affiliated with the candidates they support. 

At least half a dozen groups (and growing) aimed at drafting their favorite Democrat to run have popped up over the last few weeks, including one for Harris. These draft organizations for Harris, Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg, Ossoff, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Khanna and former Rep. Rahm Emanuel (Ill.) are gathering names and emails that have the potential to spawn more robust organizing and volunteer infrastructures for their preferred candidate if they decide to jumpstart a bid. 

And they are full steam ahead, with or without buy-in from their principal. 

Some groups, like “Team Pete PAC” are encouraging supporters to engage potential voters with host house parties and fundraisers, with an emphasis on community service, said Jennifer Holdsworth, the former campaign manager of Buttigieg’s DNC chair run, who will help lead the PAC alongside other allies of the former South Bend, Indiana, mayor.

And despite what’s bound to be an elbows-out primary, they’re not hoarding their resources — if Buttigieg isn’t the nominee, their group is happy to share them with whoever the nominee ends up being, Holdsworth said. She believes that most other Democrats are more prone to support over sniping these days anyhow. 

“I think that the field is going to be extraordinarily exciting. I’ve been in and around Democratic politics for around 25 years, and I’ve not yet seen the type of excitement at the beginning of the process this much,” Holdsworth told HuffPost. “I’m really hearing people talk about how excited they are right at the beginning, and I’m not hearing in real life a lot of sniping against any of the candidates. I think everybody is just completely moved that there’s so many people that may or may not be interested in it.”

“Ready for AOC” is also building a list of potential volunteers.

“Winning won’t be easy, but it will be worth it,” the group says. “AOC won’t have the backing of billionaire donors eager to line the pockets of candidates they know they can control. If we want AOC to win in 2028, the work starts now, and it starts with us.”

The “Run Kamala Run PAC” will host its first virtual kickoff event this Saturday, headlined by Chris Walton, former Chair of the Democratic Party of Milwaukee County, Wisconsin. The group is touting Harris as a frontrunner despite media skepticism.

“The media narrative is wrong. People like Kamala Harris, and they want her to run again,” said Matthew Taylor, president and treasurer of Run Kamala Run PAC, in a statement announcing the event. “More than 6,000 people signed up before we were even a PAC. Now we’re making it official.”
